Introduces Cargo Scan, an interactive Rust auditing tool for third-party crate review.
Frames dangerous Rust dependency behavior as effects: unsafe operations, system effects such as filesystem/network/process access, and higher-order control flow.
Uses effect analysis plus call-graph context to narrow human review to code that can actually cross a security boundary.

Reports that Cargo Scan reduced potentially dangerous audit work to a median of 0.2% of lines of code in the evaluated crates, and could automatically classify about 3.5K of the top 10K crates on crates.io as safe.
This is relevant to supply-chain review because CVE scanning alone does not answer whether an unfamiliar Rust crate behaves safely in context.
Cargo Scan sits between manual reading and broad static-analysis alerts: it tries to find the code paths a human should inspect instead of declaring an entire dependency graph trustworthy.

In ASCII and related standards, C0 names the 32 control codes in the range 0x00–0x1F. The same chart is standardized as the C0 set in ISO/IEC 6429 (and historically aligned with ECMA-6 / ECMA-48); it is not specific to Unix—Unix and POSIX use these bytes everywhere in text, ttys, and binary protocols.
ASCII/C0/... is the definition-first spine: code position, official name, hex. Tool pages (rg, xargs, find, libc) stay free to describe behavior while linking here for “what byte is this?”

Wikipedia — C0 and C1 control codes
Code position: 0x00 (binary zero). ASCII / ISO 6429 name NUL (often spelled NULL in prose). Same scalar value as Unicode U+0000 (general category Cc, “control”).
Notation: in C source, '\0' is the familiar escape for a single byte of value 0x00; NUL-terminated means a sequence of non-NUL bytes followed by one final 0x00 sentinel.

C strings: the language ABI ends strings with NUL; APIs such as strlen stop at the first 0x00. Binary data that may contain interior NULs is not representable in a classic C string without an explicit length.

Path lists on stdin: many tools default to newline- or whitespace-separated text, which breaks when paths contain spaces. A common pattern is NUL-terminated records: producers emit 0x00 between paths (see rg/--null; find -print0), and consumers read that stream with xargs -0 or similar (see xargs).

Line-oriented text: POSIX text files are usually modeled as lines separated by LF; NUL is generally not treated as “another newline” by line-based tools, so mixing NUL into what you think of as “plain text” often surprises tools and humans.

Ash is an opinionated, declarative application framework for Elixir that focuses on modeling an application's domain and deriving large amounts of application behavior from that model.
The official positioning is concise: model your domain, derive the rest.
Ash is aimed at the repetitive parts of serious application work: domain logic, authorization, filtering, sorting, pagination, relationships, APIs, and extension points.
It is commonly used with Phoenix and PostgreSQL, but is designed to slot into a normal Elixir codebase rather than replace the language or runtime.
Resources and actions - Ash describes the application primarily through resources and the actions those resources expose.
Behavior-first modeling - The framework emphasizes meaningful domain operations like :publish_post or :approve_order rather than exposing raw tables and ad hoc controller logic everywhere.
Declarative extensibility - The core framework is extended by packages for data layers, API layers, auth, admin, jobs, and other concerns.
Productivity with structure - The framework trades some low-level freedom for consistency and leverage in larger applications.
Domains act as entry points for related resources and operations.
Resources describe attributes, relationships, validations, calculations, aggregates, and policies, while actions describe reads, creates, updates, destroys, and custom workflows.
The surrounding ecosystem includes packages such as AshPostgres, AshSqlite, AshGraphql, AshJsonApi, AshPhoenix, and AshAuthentication.
Ash is a programming language -> False. It is an Elixir framework.
Ash is only an ORM -> Too small. Data access is part of the story, but the framework also covers domain actions, policies, APIs, and extensions.
Ash replaces Phoenix -> Not exactly. The official site explicitly presents it as something that works with Phoenix and Phoenix LiveView.

A mount ties a folder of remote files in a garden checkout to the place they are stored and the URL they are published at. Pages will link a mounted file by relative path, ../assets/.remote/<mount>/<file>, so Logseq shows it from disk. mise run site:build replaces ../assets/.remote/<mount>/ in each link with the mount's public base URL, and gitpa's website and RSS builds will do the same. Until the sub-issues of #347 Link B2 assets by relative path and publish them as public URLs land, most pages link the B2 URL directly.
Each garden declares its mounts in asset-mounts.toml at its root. The file's first line is a comment linking this page.
The table name under mounts is the mount's name. It matches the last folder of path.
path: the folder the files sit in, relative to the garden root, always assets/.remote/<mount>.

bucket: the B2 bucket that stores the files. Each file sits at the top level of the bucket and is named after its asset page, as Logseq/Entity/Asset/B2 describes: the page Course/Asset/Diagram/Overview/png is stored as Course___Asset___Diagram___Overview.png.
dvc: the name of the DVC remote in .dvc/config that stores backups of the files. Asset/mise/Task/fetch restores a file from that remote.
public: the base URL a published page links instead of the mount folder, with no trailing slash. A file's public URL is <public>/<file>.
source: the ghq address of the garden that owns the files, such as github.com/codekiln/logseq-encode-garden.
A garden owns a mount when the mount's files live in that garden's B2 bucket and DVC remote. Its mount has path, bucket and dvc, and public when the bucket is public.

A garden that links another garden's files borrows the mount. Its mount has path, public and source, with the same path and public as the owning garden. When Logseq/Entity/Proxy/Page/mise/Task/sync copies a page that links into a mount, it leaves the mounted file behind and writes the mount's borrowed declaration into the destination garden's asset-mounts.toml.
A mount without public is private. When a page links into a private mount, mise run site:build stops and names the page and the file, and gitpa's builds will do the same.

mise-tasks/asset/lib/mounts.py reads asset-mounts.toml and stops with an error that links this page when a mount has an unknown key, lacks a key its role needs, mixes owning and borrowing keys, or has a path other than assets/.remote/<mount>. The asset:* tasks keep each file in the folder of the mount this garden owns. mise run site:build reads the mounts through mounts.py too, and calls public_links in mounts.py to replace each link into a mount folder with the mount's public URL.
